David Yovanoff advises companies and investors on the full spectrum of corporate transactions, with a practice spanning mergers and acquisitions, private equity investments, venture financings, and day-to-day corporate counseling. He works closely with mid-market and emerging growth companies, both domestic and international, as well as private equity firms navigating complex transactions across a wide range of industries.
David brings a practical, business-oriented approach shaped by his experience managing deals from initial structuring through closing and beyond. He regularly leads private equity platform and add-on acquisitions, counsels founders and investors through venture financing rounds, and advises on strategic transactions that support long-term growth. His experience includes buy and sell-side M&A purchase agreements, rollover arrangements, and other core transaction documents, sophisticated financing arrangements, including convertible instruments and equity structures, as well as the full suite of venture financing documents such as SAFEs, convertible notes, and NVCA preferred stock financings.
In addition to his transactional work, David serves as outside general counsel to high-growth companies at various stages of development—from bootstrapped startups to venture-backed businesses—providing ongoing guidance on corporate governance, strategic planning, and operational matters. His clients span industries including digital advertising, technology, tech-enabled healthcare, consumer products, cannabis beverages, and industrial manufacturing.
David’s perspective is further informed by his role as a partner in a venture capital firm focused on investments in SaaS, consumer products, and tech-enabled healthcare. This dual vantage point allows him to advise clients with a strong understanding of both legal and investor considerations.
At PLG, David partners with clients to deliver thoughtful, efficient, and business-focused counsel across the lifecycle of their most important transactions.

title: Wild Horse and Burro Management: Overview of Costs
content:
A fourth question is how to increase nonfederal funding for management of wild horses and burros. Recent initiatives include BLM establishment of a "micro-donations website." Also, the BLM Wild Horse and Burro Advisory Board has recommended that the Foundation for America's Public Lands, BLM's official charitable partner, serve as a funding source/mechanism for off-range holding. [...] FY2024 Obligations by Activity
Figure 2 shows FY2024 BLM obligations of wild horse and burro funding of $153.3 million, by activity. Off-range holding accounted for $101.4 million (66%), composed of $70.9 million (46%) for short-term care and $30.5 million (20%) for long-term care. Program support and adoptions and sales were each 10%. Other portions were 5% for gathering (animals on the range), 4% for growth suppression, and 5% for other activities.

It is unclear whether funding levels have been appropriate to care for wild horses and burros. Program costs would vary based on the overall management strategy adopted and the particular programs emphasized (e.g., off-range holding, adoption, or population control). For instance, 2018 and 2020 BLM reports (and a 2020 fact sheet) presented management options with varying associated costs.

Wild Horse and Burro Management: Overview of Costs
Updated January 15, 2026 (IF11060) 
Background
The Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 (1971 Act, 16 U.S.C. §§1331 et seq.) provides for management and protection of wild horses and burros by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), within the Department of the Interior, and the Forest Service (FS), within the Department of Agriculture. For decades, federal management of wild horses and burros in western states has generated controversy, study, proposals, and lawsuits on occasion. BLM and FS use several approaches to achieve the _appropriate management level_ (AML) of animals on the range, including placement into private care (primarily adoption and sale), off-range holding, and fertility control,among others. Management costs have increased over time (Figure 1). Issues for Congress include the adequacy and use of funding to achieve AML, primarily on BLM lands.
Overview of Authority
Under the 1971 Act, BLM and FS inventory horse and burro populations periodically to determine AML for each herd. When the pertinent Secretary determines that an overpopulation exists and that it is necessary to remove excess animals, the law requires specific actions (16 U.S.C. §1333(b)(2)). First, the Secretary "shall order old, sick, or lame animals to be destroyed in the most humane manner possible." Second, the Secretary "shall cause ... excess ... horses and burros to be humanely captured" for private adoption. Third, where there is no adoption demand, the Secretary shall cause excess animals "to be destroyed in the most humane and cost efficient manner possible."
Congress has enacted additional authorities to reduce excess animals. For instance, P.L. 108-447, Division E, Section 142, authorized excess animal sales, with provisions to (1) direct the agencies to sell, "without limitation," excess animals (or remains) that are more than 10 years old or offered for adoption unsuccessfully at least three times; (2) remove a ban on sale of wild horses and burros (and remains) for processing into commercial products; and (3) remove criminal penalties for processing the remains of a sold animal into commercial products.
Since 1982, BLM and FS have not used their authority to destroy healthy animals. Further, most (but not all) annual Interior appropriations laws over the past few decades have prohibited BLM from using funds therein for destruction of healthy animals or for sales of animals that result in processing into commercial products. Since FY2020, Interior appropriations laws typically contained a similar FS provision (e.g., P.L. 118-42, Division E, §417(e)).
Population
Achieving and maintaining the number of wild horses and burros at the national AML has challenged BLM for decades. As of March 1, 2025, BLM had set the AML upper limit for all wild horse and burro herds on its lands at 25,556 animals, but the on-range estimate was 73,130 animals. However, this level is 23% less than the 2020 recent high of 95,114 animals, due to factors including increased removals, adoptions/sales, and fertility control.
BLM manages wild horses and burros in 175 herd management areas (HMAs) in 10 western states. Nearly half (83) of the HMAs are in Nevada. Wyoming, Oregon, Utah, and California each have between 14 and 21 HMAs. BLM also manages thousands of these animals—64,205 as of August 2025—off range. During periodic gathers and removals, these additional animals were removed from rangelands exceeding AML. Most (61%) are being cared for in long-term (pasture) facilities, typically for the remainder of their lives. Others (39%) are in short-term (corral) facilities, usually to be readied for adoption or sale. For FS lands, AML is roughly 3,500 (January 2025). The number on range—about 9,000-9,500—is more than double the AML. The animals are on 34 active territories in several states, with about two dozen managed jointly with BLM.
Wild Horse and Burro Program Funding
It is unclear whether funding levels have been appropriate to care for wild horses and burros. Program costs would vary based on the overall management strategy adopted and the particular programs emphasized (e.g., off-range holding, adoption, or population control). For instance, 2018 and 2020 BLM reports (and a 2020 fact sheet) presented management options with varying associated costs.

BLM Historical Appropriations: FY2000-FY2025
The FY2025 appropriation for BLM management of wild horses and burros was $142.0 million. Relative to FY2000 ($20.4 million), this was nearly a 600% increase in nominal dollars and about a 270% increase in 2025 dollars. The FY2025 appropriation also was about 4% less than the FY2023 peak of $147.9 million in nominal dollars and about 9% less in 2025 dollars (Figure 1). FS wild horse and burro appropriations are not separately identifiable.
Since FY2000, appropriations laws periodically have provided BLM funding to reduce animals on the range. For example, in FY2010, BLM received $64.0 million, compared with $40.6 million in FY2009. The increase was for activities (e.g., removal and adoption of animals, population control) to achieve AML by 2013 (which did not occur) and for the escalating cost of long-term holding. As another example, the FY2022 appropriation was $137.1 million, compared with $115.7 million in FY2021, to support "an aggressive, non-lethal population control strategy" as set out in BLM's 2020 report, according to the explanatory statement. This strategy was to include increased removals, long-term holding, and fertility control.
FY2024 Obligations by Activity
Figure 2 shows FY2024 BLM obligations of wild horse and burro funding of $153.3 million, by activity. Off-range holding accounted for $101.4 million (66%), composed of $70.9 million (46%) for short-term care and $30.5 million (20%) for long-term care. Program support and adoptions and sales were each 10%. Other portions were 5% for gathering (animals on the range), 4% for growth suppression, and 5% for other activities.

Issues and Proposals Related to Costs
Concerns over increasing wild horse and burro populations and program costs have prompted studies and proposals for years. In response to congressional direction, BLM issued a report in 2020proposing actions to achieve AML over 15-18 years. The emphasis was on animal removals, off-range holding, placement into private care, and fertility control and included related costs. Some Appropriations Committee reports have expressed an intent to fund options in BLM's 2020 report.
Some questions pertain to how to increase the number, and reduce the average cost, of animals placed in private care. BLM has sought to increase adoptions and sales by partnering with organizations (including new partnerships). BLM typically charges a minimum of $25 to adopt or purchase an untrained animal and $125 per trained animal, but BLM estimated the average cost to the agency at about $1,700 in 2025. This cost includes making the animals more marketable (e.g., by training, advertising, and transporting) but excludes a $1,000 adoption incentive thatended in March 2025. The cost of placement in private care is considerably less than BLM's average lifetime cost of caring for an animal—about $15,000%20estimates,to%20care%20for%20unadopted%20and%20unsold%20animals) in 2025. This was a decrease from $27,500 in 2023, according to BLM, due to the acquisition of additional long-term pasture facilities, which are lower cost than short-term corral facilities.
However, the number of animals in short-term facilities has increased (e.g., by 54% from 16,325 in 2021 to 25,110 in 2025). Another question is whether animals can be moved more quickly from short-term corral facilities into long-term pasture facilities to achieve program savings. Long-term holding typically is used for older and other animals with less potential for adoption or sale, with an average cost in 2025 at about $2.35 per animal per day, according to BLM. The cost of short-term corral facilities was about $6 per animal per day in 2025. Short-term facilities are more expensive due in part to hay costs, veterinary services, and farrier services to prepare the animals for adoption or sale and, in some cases, to the costs of BLM salaried employees.
A third question—how to improve fertility control to reduce herd sizes and costs—has been a focus of BLM research and was recommended by BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Advisory Board. BLM estimated the cost of the most common method—Porcine Zona Pellucida (PZP) vaccines—at $2,100 per mare in 2025, including gathering, treating with PZP, holding for a short time, and then releasing back to the range. PZP generally is most effective for one year only. To lower costs, areas of research have included longer-lasting fertility control. Since 2018, BLM has increased use of the GonaCon-Equine vaccine, which can produce four or more years of infertility in mares receiving a booster dose. The cost of this treatment was about $2,500 per mare in 2025, including the vaccine; application by dart or gather/treat/hold/release; and staff travel and labor.
A fourth question is how to increase nonfederal funding for management of wild horses and burros. Recent initiatives include BLM establishment of a "micro-donations website." Also, the BLM Wild Horse and Burro Advisory Board has recommended that the Foundation for America's Public Lands, BLM's official charitable partner, serve as a funding source/mechanism for off-range holding.
A fifth question is whether BLM should sell excess animals without limitations and/or destroy excess healthy animals to reduce program costs, as some observers have proposed. President Trump's FY2026 budget did not prohibit use of funds for destruction of animals. Also, the FY2020 BLM budget justification had called for availability of all authorities under the 1971 Act by removing sale limitations (intended as safeguards against slaughter) and prohibitions on using funds to destroy healthy animals. The FY2020 appropriations law retained these provisions.

SUMMARY
Robotics funding is rising sharply in 2026, but the market is splitting in two: more companies are raising money, while most of the extra capital is flowing into very large rounds tied to production, deployment and Physical AI.
Deal activity is genuinely broader. We tracked 116 financings across 107 companies, up from 94 deals across 90 companies a year earlier, so the expansion is not just the same few startups raising again.
The $7.26 billion headline overstates how strong the ordinary fundraising market feels. Excluding rounds above $50 million, 2026 funding falls to $882 million, below the $1.02 billion recorded over the same period in 2025.
The more unusual change is the thickness of the upper end of the market. Twenty-three known rounds sit in the $100 million-plus bucket, while the top five deals still account for roughly the same share of total capital as last year.
Physical AI and Collaborative Robots are at the center of that shift. Collaborative Robots represent 21.6% of deals but 51.8% of known capital, with a median financing of $140 million.
Early-stage robotics has not disappeared. Seed and Series A still account for more than half of 2026 deals, and first financings increased to 26, but the size gap between first rounds and follow-ons has become enormous.
The market is increasingly rewarding companies that can show a path from prototype to deployment. Apptronik, NEURA Robotics, Mind Robotics and Walden Robotics all illustrate how quickly capital requirements rise once manufacturing, fleet deployment and real-world data collection enter the picture.
Asia-Pacific has the strongest breadth story this year. Its share of robotics deals rose to 47.4%, driven largely by China and India, and even sub-$50 million known capital in the region more than doubled from the comparable 2025 period.
Europe and North America still produce many of the biggest checks, but their smaller-round funding is weaker. Corporate investors are also more involved again, especially where they can provide factories, customers, chips, engineering support or deployment environments alongside capital.
Robotics has already surpassed the full-year capital totals recorded for both 2024 and 2025, yet the most important trend is not simply “more money.” The market is getting broader in company count while becoming much more aggressive at the scale-up end, where credible real-world deployment can unlock financing in the hundreds of millions.

Is robotics funding really booming in 2026?
Robotics funding is clearly having a much stronger year in 2026, although the $7.26 billion headline makes the improvement look broader than it really is.
We tracked 116 robotics financings from January 1 through September 21, compared with 94 over the same period in 2025 and 89 in 2024. The number of funded companies also climbed from 90 to 107 in one year. So there is more activity today, and more companies are benefiting from it.
Capital has moved much faster. Quantifiable funding reached $7.26 billion, up 132% from $3.14 billion over the comparable 2025 period. The median round increased too, from $12 million to $14.7 million, so the typical disclosed financing has become somewhat larger.
The average round tells a very different story. It almost doubled to $73.4 million. The gap between a $14.7 million median and a $73.4 million average shows what is really happening: 2026 has produced a much thicker layer of very large robotics rounds.

Are more robotics startups actually getting funded now?
Yes. More robotics companies are getting funded today, and that is one of the strongest parts of the 2026 story.
The 116 financings we found went to 107 different companies. A year earlier, 94 deals were spread across 90 companies. Deal activity and company breadth are rising together rather than being created by the same handful of startups repeatedly coming back for money.
Repeated fundraising is still becoming more common. Eight companies completed more than one round during the 2026 period, compared with four in 2025 and only one in 2024.
Mind Robotics is the outlier. The young industrial-robotics company raised $500 million in March and another $400 million two months later. But cases like Mind do not explain the rise from 90 to 107 funded companies. The market itself has widened.
That makes the current robotics cycle more interesting than a simple megaround boom. More startups are entering the funded population at the same time as a smaller group moves into a completely different financing league.

Would robotics funding still look strong without the megadeals?
No. Strip away the biggest robotics rounds and the apparent capital boom largely disappears.
Funding below $50 million comes to $882 million so far in 2026, down from $1.02 billion over the same period last year. Even after using a much higher $100 million cutoff, the remaining capital is $1.38 billion versus $1.54 billion in 2025.
The middle of the market has not collapsed. The median round is higher than last year, and sub-$20 million financings still make up more than half of the deals where we know the amount. But the explosive growth sits much further up the distribution.
Almost one in four quantifiable 2026 rounds reached at least $100 million. The comparable figure last year was roughly one in eleven.
What is striking is that concentration at the very top has barely changed. The biggest five rounds account for 42.9% of capital today, almost identical to 43.1% last year. The difference is the number of companies sitting just below that top tier. Large robotics rounds have become much more common rather than simply much more concentrated.

Why are $100 million robotics rounds suddenly so common?
Robotics companies are currently raising hundreds of millions because the expensive part of the race has shifted from building impressive prototypes to manufacturing, deploying and training robots at scale.
NEURA Robotics gives us the clearest example. Its Series C of up to $1.4 billion is meant to support serial production, international expansion and a network of NEURA Gyms where robots can train on real-world tasks.
The company has kept pushing that strategy since the financing. It announced a new NEURA Gym with RWTH Aachen in July, acquired Bosch Rexroth's ACTIVE Shuttle platform in August and added ADLATUS Robotics later that month. In September, NEURA and SECO announced work on compute modules, manufacturing and industrial data for Physical AI systems.
Apptronik is heading in the same direction. Its $520 million extension brought its Series A above $935 million. The company says the capital will help scale production and deployment of Apollo humanoids. It has since expanded Robot Park, where fleets of Apollo 2 robots collect real-world training data across Apptronik sites and customer environments.
Walden Robotics makes the economics even easier to see. The company launched from stealth with $300 million and said its robots were already doing production work at a Toyota plant in North America. Toyota co-led the financing, while NVIDIA, Boeing, Samsung Ventures and Prologis Ventures participated.
These companies need much more than engineers and model-training compute. They are paying for hardware, factories, fleets, deployment sites, data collection and integration into industrial workflows. Once investors believe a robotics company is ready to move beyond pilots, the financing requirement can jump very quickly.

Is Physical AI becoming the center of robotics funding?
Yes. Physical AI and Collaborative Robots have become the clearest magnet for robotics capital this year.
Collaborative Robots represent 21.6% of the deals we tracked but 51.8% of quantifiable funding. A year earlier, the category accounted for just 9.6% of deals and 12.2% of capital. Its median round has climbed from $50 million to $140 million.
The change goes well beyond terminology. NEURA is building real-world training facilities around its Physical AI platform. Apptronik is collecting robot data through Robot Park and working with Google DeepMind. Walden describes itself as a full-stack Physical AI company focused first on manufacturing and logistics.
Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics work also helps explain why this area is attracting so much attention. Its robotics models are designed to connect vision, language, spatial reasoning and physical actions, and Apptronik is one of the companies working with Google DeepMind on humanoid systems.
There is still a lot of concentration inside the category. NEURA alone represents roughly 37% of known Collaborative Robots capital, while the three largest deals account for around 62%.
Even with that concentration, the rotation is hard to miss. Investors are putting far more money into robots that combine general-purpose hardware, AI models and learning from real-world environments than they were a year ago.

Are early-stage robotics startups getting squeezed?
Early-stage robotics is less dominant than it was last year, but the data does not look like a broad early-stage funding freeze.
Seed and Series A together represent 54.3% of 2026 deals, down from 66.0% over the same period in 2025. On its own, that looks like a strong move toward later-stage funding.
The 2024 comparison changes the interpretation. Early-stage deals represented 51.7% of the market two years ago, slightly below where they sit now. In other words, 2025 was unusually early-stage-heavy.
There is another reason not to push the conclusion too far. Unknown stages now account for 16.4% of deals, almost twice their 2025 share. With that much missing stage information, the exact shift toward later stages is harder to measure.
What we can see clearly is the widening difference in round size. Seed carries a $3.52 million median, Series A $18 million and Series B $50 million. By Series C, the median has reached $104.9 million.
The current robotics market still funds plenty of young companies. The real change is how quickly the financing scale can jump once a company moves into the group investors believe is ready to industrialize.

Are investors still funding new robotics startups, or mostly backing existing winners?
Investors are still funding new robotics companies, but most of the money now goes to startups that have already raised before.
We found 26 first financings in 2026, up from 20 last year and just 10 over the comparable 2024 period. First financings now represent 22.4% of all deals, almost unchanged from 21.3% in 2025.
So new-company formation still looks healthy. The separation appears once we look at check sizes.
A first financing has a median size of $3.8 million. Follow-on rounds have reached a $23.95 million median, more than six times higher. Follow-ons account for about $6.85 billion of capital, compared with roughly $418 million for first financings.
Walden is an extraordinary exception. It launched with a $300 million seed round, backed by Toyota and a group of major strategic and financial investors. Most new robotics companies start much closer to the $3.8 million median.
Mind Robotics shows how quickly the gap can widen after that first round. Founded in 2025, the company raised $115 million initially, followed by $500 million and then $400 million in 2026.
Robotics is still creating new funded companies. The current market simply rewards a small number of emerging winners with capital at a speed and scale that make the rest of the startup population look tiny by comparison.

Are the biggest robotics checks going to older companies?
Surprisingly, no. The typical funded robotics company is younger this year even though the biggest rounds have become much larger.
The median company receiving funding in 2026 is around four years old, compared with five years in both 2025 and 2024.
The stage progression itself remains intuitive. Seed companies have a median age of two years, Series A companies four, Series B companies five and Series C companies nine.
What has changed is how quickly some companies can reach enormous financing rounds. Mind Robotics was founded in 2025 and crossed $1 billion in cumulative funding within months. Walden was created in 2026 and launched with $300 million.
Collaborative Robots also has a median company age of only three years, even though it currently attracts the largest rounds in the market.
That is a pretty unusual feature of 2026. Huge robotics rounds no longer automatically mean we are looking at ten-year-old companies moving slowly through the traditional venture ladder. Investors are sometimes financing industrial scale almost immediately.
Is Asia taking over robotics deal flow?
Asia-Pacific has become the biggest source of robotics deals in our research this year, and the shift looks much broader than a handful of giant Chinese rounds.
The region now represents 47.4% of transactions, up from 20.2% in 2025. We counted 55 Asia-Pacific deals compared with 19 last year.
China explains much of that jump. It went from 11 transactions in the comparable 2025 period to 32 this year. India moved from five to 11.
The capital figures require more care because only 38 of those 55 Asia-Pacific deals have a usable amount. Several large Chinese rounds were disclosed with minimum values or ranges, so we left them out of calculations that require a defensible single number.
Even after removing rounds above $50 million, known Asia-Pacific capital increased from $143 million to $326 million. That makes the geographic expansion harder to dismiss as a megaround effect.
China is also giving robotics companies more places to test and deploy their technology. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the state-assets regulator launched a 2026 program for humanoid robots and embodied AI in real production and everyday environments, with targets around application validation, regular deployment and real-machine data collection.
The government has also been moving into standards. Recent work covers humanoid training grounds, applications such as substations and a dedicated humanoid-robot and embodied-intelligence standardization committee.
Private capital is moving alongside that push. Galaxea AI, for example, raised about $291 million in April at a valuation above RMB20 billion. Caixin described Chinese robotics investment as increasingly concentrating around a smaller group of leading companies.
The policy environment does not explain every deal, but the combination of higher deal volume, private capital and real-world deployment programs makes China's current rise hard to write off as hype.

Is Europe really having a robotics funding boom?
Europe is having a huge year for robotics megadeals, while the smaller European funding market is actually weaker than it was last year.
Quantifiable European capital reached about $2.23 billion, up from $596 million over the comparable 2025 period. Remove rounds above $50 million and European funding falls from $292 million last year to $226 million today.
NEURA's round of up to $1.4 billion explains a large part of that difference. The financing brought together Tether, Qualcomm Technologies, Amazon, NVIDIA, Bosch, Schaeffler, the European Investment Bank and other investors.
The European Investment Bank separately records a €40 million financing signed with NEURA in 2026, tied to the company's development of cognitive and humanoid robotics.
Europe is clearly capable of producing and financing very large robotics companies right now. What we have not found is the same acceleration across ordinary European rounds.
North America has a related problem. It still leads the market in known capital at 39.8%, helped by companies such as Apptronik, Mind Robotics and Walden, but its capital excluding rounds above $50 million dropped from $589 million to $323 million.
Asia currently has the stronger breadth story. Europe and North America still produce many of the largest checks.

Are corporate investors becoming more important in robotics?
Corporate and industrial investors are playing a bigger role in robotics again, particularly in the rounds tied to manufacturing and deployment.
Strategic investors participated in 42 of the 116 deals we tracked, equal to 36.2% of the market. That is up from 29.8% in 2025, although still below the 42.7% recorded in 2024.
The size of those deals has changed much more. A robotics round with strategic participation has a $70 million median this year, compared with $27.85 million in 2025.
The names help explain why these investors matter. NVIDIA, Bosch, Schaeffler, Baidu, Lens Technology, Meituan Dragonball and Prologis Ventures all appear more than once in our 2026 research.
Apptronik has backing from Google, Mercedes-Benz, John Deere and other large groups. Mercedes-Benz has also been testing Apptronik's Apollo humanoids in manufacturing environments. Walden's investors include Toyota, NVIDIA, Boeing, Samsung Ventures and Prologis Ventures.
This kind of capital can come with factories, customers, chips, engineering expertise or deployment environments. For a robotics company trying to prove that a machine works reliably outside the lab, those relationships can be as useful as the money itself.
The lead-investor market remains much less concentrated. We found 125 disclosed leads or co-leads this year, compared with 92 in 2025, while only four led more than one deal. There is plenty of investor breadth underneath the concentration in round size.

Has 2026 already beaten previous full years for robotics funding?
Yes. Robotics funding in 2026 has already passed the full-year capital totals we recorded for both 2025 and 2024.
The $7.26 billion of quantifiable capital through September 21 is equal to about 144% of the $5.05 billion recorded during all of 2025 and roughly 230% of 2024's $3.17 billion.
Deal volume is much closer. The 116 transactions recorded so far equal about 85% of the 136 deals completed during all of 2025. The market has already exceeded the 112 deals recorded across the entirety of 2024.
We would not project those figures mechanically through the end of the year. Robotics funding is too lumpy for that, especially when individual deals can reach several hundred million dollars.
There is also a data-quality wrinkle worth keeping visible. We have usable amounts for 85.3% of 2026 rounds, compared with more than 91% in both previous comparable periods. Seventeen 2026 financings have no usable amount, including several reported only as minimum values.
For now, the conclusion is still unusually strong: 2026 has already become the most capital-intensive robotics year in this three-year comparison, even before accounting for some incompletely disclosed rounds.
What is actually driving the robotics funding shift?
The robotics funding shift is being driven by the move from prototypes toward production, deployment and continuous real-world learning.
Several of the biggest 2026 financings point in the same direction. NEURA is using its capital for serial production and Physical AI training infrastructure. Apptronik is scaling Apollo manufacturing and building real-world data collection through Robot Park. Mind Robotics is working around industrial automation and factory data. Walden started with a direct connection to Toyota production environments.
China's recent policy work follows the same logic. The focus is increasingly on real production sites, application validation, training environments, data collection and repeatable deployment rather than laboratory capability alone.
AI progress is part of the explanation too. Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics work is aimed at giving robots stronger spatial reasoning, generalization and physical-action capabilities. That does not solve manufacturing or reliability, but it makes investors more willing to believe that software improvement can compound after robots are deployed.
This changes what a well-funded robotics company looks like. The most ambitious startups now need an AI stack, capable hardware, manufacturing capacity, access to real environments and enough deployed robots to create useful training data.
Building all of that at once is expensive. These days, investors appear willing to finance it when they see a credible path from the robot demo to the factory floor.

What should robotics founders take away from the funding market today?
Robotics founders can still raise early money today, but the really large pools of capital are increasingly reserved for companies that can show how their technology will work in the real world at scale.
There were 63 Seed and Series A deals in our research period, so the market has plenty of room for new companies. First financings are also more numerous than they were one or two years ago.
The harder transition comes after the product works. Investors now have some very expensive reference points for what scale can look like: Apollo moving through industrial deployment, NEURA building training infrastructure, Walden already working inside Toyota production and Chinese humanoid companies racing into real-world testing.
A startup does not need to build a humanoid robot to fit that pattern. Warehouse robotics, surgical systems, agricultural robots and infrastructure machines continue to attract capital.
What investors increasingly want to understand is much simpler: who will use the robot, where it will work, how reliably it can perform the task, how many units can be built and whether every deployment makes the system better.
That is where the financing market looks strongest right now.
What is actually changing in robotics funding?
Robotics funding is stronger in 2026 because more companies are getting financed and the market has produced far more very large rounds.
The broadest change is activity. Deal count is up 23% and unique funded companies are up 19% from the same period last year. We are looking at a larger funded ecosystem, not merely bigger checks going to an unchanged group of companies.
The capital boom is much narrower. Once the rounds above $50 million are taken out, funding is below last year's level. The ordinary robotics startup is operating in a much more normal fundraising market than the $7.26 billion headline suggests.
Physical AI and Collaborative Robots have become the biggest area of rotation. They are gaining both deals and capital, while the $140 million category median shows how aggressively investors are funding companies they think can reach large-scale deployment.
New robotics startups are still getting financed. The real split is between company formation and scale-up: first rounds remain relatively small, while follow-on capital can move into the hundreds of millions extremely quickly.
Asia-Pacific has produced the clearest geographic expansion. China in particular is adding far more funded companies while government programs push humanoid robots and embodied AI into real environments. Europe and North America remain major sources of megadeals, but their smaller-round funding has weakened.
Corporate participation is another important part of the current cycle. Manufacturers, chip companies, technology platforms and logistics groups are increasingly appearing alongside financial investors in rounds built around production and deployment.
The apparent move away from early stage needs more caution. Early-stage share has fallen sharply from 2025, but it remains slightly above 2024 and the rise in unknown stages makes the exact shift harder to measure.
The clearest trend is this: robotics capital is moving toward companies that investors believe can turn AI-powered machines into deployed industrial systems, and the cost of making that jump is creating a new class of exceptionally large private financings.

OUR METHODOLOGY
This analysis measures current robotics funding by comparing qualifying financings announced from January 1 through September 21, 2026 with the same January 1 through September 21 periods in 2025 and 2024. Full-year 2024 and 2025 figures are used only where they add secondary context and are identified as full-year comparisons.
We built the dataset from company and investor announcements, government and regulatory records, reputable financial and technology reporting, and established funding databases. Where several credible sources were available, we cross-checked material facts such as financing date, amount, stage, investors and company status.
We used a strict robotics-market definition. A company had to be overwhelmingly focused on robotics as its core business at the time of the financing. Borderline companies were excluded rather than added simply because robotics appeared somewhere in their product roadmap.
We included qualifying private-company equity financings and excluded debt, grants, loans, public offerings, unconverted convertibles, SAFEs and financings where an equity component could not be isolated reliably. Separate financings were counted separately, while duplicate reports of the same round were consolidated and extensions, additional closes and tranches were reviewed individually.
We did not infer funding stages from round size, assume that a prominent investor was the lead, or estimate undisclosed deal amounts. Minimum amounts and vague ranges were preserved as such and excluded from calculations that require a defensible single number.
First-financing versus follow-on status is based on a separate public funding-history check. The distinction is useful for directional analysis, but it should not be read as a perfect reconstruction of every historical financing completed by every company.
After compiling the dataset, we ran a separate quality-control pass for missed deals, date boundaries, duplicate rounds, equity eligibility, robotics-market fit, category consistency and unusual financing structures. The final 2026 dataset contains 116 qualifying financings, with a usable financing amount for 99 of them, or 85.3%.
Key sources include NEURA Robotics on its Series C and deployment strategy, Apptronik on its Series A financing, Apptronik on Robot Park and real-world training data, Walden Robotics on its $300 million launch financing, TechCrunch on Mind Robotics' $500 million financing, TechCrunch on Mind Robotics' additional $400 million round, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology on 2026 humanoid-robot and embodied-AI deployment, the European Investment Bank on its NEURA financing, Google DeepMind on Gemini Robotics, Mercedes-Benz on Apollo testing in manufacturing, and Caixin Global on Galaxea AI and Chinese robotics investment.

 Corporate investors are deeply involved in robotics funding. Google, Mercedes-Benz, NVIDIA, Microsoft, FedEx, LG Electronics, Walmart and other strategic groups repeatedly invest alongside traditional venture capital firms.
 Public markets are becoming an ongoing source of robotics financing. Companies including Symbotic, Serve Robotics, PROCEPT BioRobotics, Vicarious Surgical and Dobot have continued raising equity after reaching public markets.

A few word about our methodology
As you can see, we built a database that ranks robotics startups based on their total cumulative fundraising. To create this ranking, we reviewed many sources and cross-checked information across multiple places.
Whenever possible, we prioritized official company communications, since they are the most reliable source for robotics funding amounts. When those were not available, we relied on reputable industry sources such as TechCrunch, Crunchbase, Financial Times or Forbes (to name a few).
We excluded random blogs, unverified websites, and any sources that could not be validated.
We focused on equity fundraising and excluded transactions that did not represent qualifying equity capital raised by the robotics company.
When funding rounds were announced in other currencies such as euros, Swiss francs, Singapore dollars, Australian dollars, or rupees, we converted them into approximate USD equivalents for consistency.
Sometimes different sources report slightly different numbers, or the exact round size is not fully disclosed. In those cases, we flag the uncertainty and assign a confidence label to each robotics startup, visible in the last column.
Here is what they mean.
Full confidence: The company’s equity fundraising history can be reconstructed completely from public sources. The rounds, dates, amounts, and key investors are clearly identified, with no meaningful gaps.
Strong confidence: The fundraising history is largely complete and reliable. There may be a small missing detail, such as incomplete investor information or a minor round with limited data, but the overall record is clear.
Partial confidence: The main fundraising rounds can be identified, but the record is incomplete or somewhat mixed. Some rounds may be missing or certain funding events may be difficult to separate clearly.
Low confidence: Public information is too limited, inconsistent, or ambiguous to reliably reconstruct the company’s equity fundraising history.
When the confidence level is too low, we take a conservative approach and exclude the company from the ranking. We don’t want to include data that cannot be reliably verified.
This reflects how we conduct all our research, including the work behind our report covering the robotics market.
In a world where LLMs hallucinate and unreliable information is everywhere, our goal is simple: provide data you can trust.
If you want the full detail on a specific calculation, feel free to contact us and we will gladly explain.
Finally, know that we update the dataset once per month, so come back here if you need fresh information.

At New Market Pitch, we kept seeing the same problem: when you look at a new market, the data is either missing, paywalled, or buried in 300-page reports that feel like they were written in the 80s. On the other side, LLMs and random blog posts give you confident answers with no sources, and sometimes they just make things up. That’s not good enough when you’re about to invest real money or launch a company.
So we decided to fix the experience. For each market we cover, we build a structured database and update it on a regular basis. We track funding rounds, fund memos, M&A moves, partnerships, new products, policy changes, and the real activity of startups and incumbents. Then we turn all of that into a clear “market pitch” that shows where the opportunities are and how people actually win in that space.
Every key data point is checked, sourced, and put back into context by our team. That’s how we can give you both speed and reliability: fast coverage of new markets, without the usual guesswork.
